Q001420.stem: A team is building one assistant that must reason step by step and decide at runtime which of three Python tools to call (a calculator, a web search function, and an inventory lookup running on AWS Lambda). The agent runs in the team's own container on Amazon ECS, and the team wants the foundation model, not hand-written branching logic, to drive tool selection with minimal orchestration code. There is no need to route between multiple specialized agents. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Model the reasoning loop as an AWS Step Functions state machine with a Choice state per tool, invoked from the container
Create an Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flow that chains the three tools in a fixed order for every request
Use AWS Agent Squad to classify each request and route it to one of three specialized agents, one per tool
Build it with the Strands Agents SDK, registering the Python functions as tools for the model to choose

Q001420.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for model-driven agents. You declare Python functions as tools, and the SDK runs the reason-act loop: the model reads the tool descriptions, picks a tool, receives the result, and decides the next step. It runs anywhere Python runs, including a container on ECS, with very little boilerplate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Agent Squad: built to route requests across multiple specialized agents. The scenario has one agent with several tools, so this adds an unnecessary routing layer.
• Step Functions with Choice states: the branching logic is hand-written, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid. The model would no longer decide the next tool.
• Prompt Flow in a fixed order: a flow is a predefined DAG. It cannot choose tools dynamically based on intermediate results.

Key takeaway: one agent with many tools and model-driven selection → Strands Agents. Many specialist agents that need request routing → Agent Squad or Bedrock multi-agent collaboration.

Q001423.stem: An agent first asks the model to write a complete five-step plan and then executes all steps in order. When step 2 returns an unexpected result (for example, the customer record is not found), the agent still runs steps 3-5 and produces a wrong answer. The team wants the model to reason about each observation before choosing the next action. Which prompting pattern should replace the current design?

choices.text: ReAct, interleaving a reasoning step, a tool call, and the resulting observation on every iteration
Chain-of-thought prompting that asks the model to think step by step before producing the whole plan
Self-consistency sampling, generating several plans and executing the most common one
Plan-and-execute with a more detailed upfront plan that lists every possible branch in advance

Q001423.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ReAct (Reason + Act) makes the model alternate between thinking, calling a tool, and reading the observation. Because each next action is chosen after seeing the latest tool result, an unexpected result in step 2 changes the following steps instead of being ignored.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A more detailed upfront plan: still commits to actions before seeing results. Enumerating every branch in advance is brittle and does not scale.
• Chain-of-thought before planning: improves the quality of the plan, but the plan is still fixed and never revisited after tool results arrive.
• Self-consistency: picks the most common of several plans. It improves robustness of the reasoning, but still executes a fixed plan without reacting to observations.

Key takeaway: when the next action depends on what the previous tool returned, use an observe-then-act loop (ReAct), not a fixed plan.

Q001428.stem: An agent built with a tool-calling framework keeps making two kinds of mistakes: it passes the string 'twenty dollars' to a refund tool that expects a numeric amount, and it calls getOrderStatus when the user asks about a package's shipping location. The tool code is correct when called with valid inputs. What is the MOST effective fix?

choices.text: Add a Bedrock guardrail denied topic for shipping questions so the model stops calling the wrong tool
Lower the temperature to 0 so the model always produces the same parameters and tool choice
Tighter tool specs: typed required parameters and when-to-use descriptions
Attach an IAM policy to the agent's role that denies refund calls unless the amount parameter is numeric

Q001428.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The model decides which tool to call and how to fill its arguments from the tool specification: name, description, and parameter schema. A typed schema (for example, amount: number, currency: string, both required) steers argument formatting, and a description that states when to use and not use each tool fixes selection mistakes between similar tools.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policy on the parameter: IAM authorizes AWS API calls. It cannot validate the arguments the model generates for your own tool.
• Guardrail denied topic: would block legitimate shipping questions entirely instead of routing them to the right tool.
• Temperature 0: makes output more repeatable, but repeatably wrong if the specification is ambiguous.

Key takeaway: most tool-selection and argument errors are specification problems. Fix the schema and descriptions first, then validate arguments in code.

Q001433.stem: A company runs a claims assistant on one Bedrock foundation model with steady traffic 24 hours a day. Even with retries, it sees ThrottlingException errors during daily peaks. A regulator requires that inference stays in a single Region. The company needs guaranteed capacity for this model and accepts a term commitment. Which option meets all requirements?

choices.text: Move the peak traffic to Bedrock batch inference so that it does not count against on-demand quotas
Request a higher on-demand tokens-per-minute quota and keep invoking the model on demand
Invoke the model through a global cross-Region inference profile to draw on capacity in other Regions
Purchase Bedrock Provisioned Throughput for the model in that Region

Q001433.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model units for a specific model in a specific Region, so the committed capacity is not shared with other on-demand callers. It fits steady, predictable load when the company is willing to commit to a term.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Global cross-Region inference: adds burst capacity, but routes requests to other Regions, which violates the single-Region requirement.
• Batch inference: asynchronous and results arrive later, so it cannot serve an interactive claims assistant.
• Higher on-demand quota: raises the ceiling you are allowed to request, but on-demand capacity is still shared and not guaranteed.

Key takeaway: guaranteed capacity plus a residency constraint plus steady load → Provisioned Throughput. Burst relief without a commitment → cross-Region inference, if residency rules allow it.

Q001439.stem: A marketplace classifies 5 million short product reviews per day into five sentiment classes. Each classification must return within 300 ms to support live moderation. A large general-purpose model reaches 94% accuracy. A smaller model fine-tuned (or distilled) on labeled reviews reaches 93% at about 1/15 of the cost. The business requires at least 92% accuracy. Which approach is BEST?

choices.text: Send reviews to the large model through batch inference overnight to get the batch discount
Keep the large model and buy Provisioned Throughput to lower the effective per-request price
Keep the large model and enable prompt caching on the classification instructions to cut cost
Serve the smaller fine-tuned or distilled model, which meets the accuracy floor and latency target

Q001439.explanation:
Why this is correct:
For a narrow, well-defined task, a smaller specialized model often gets within a point of a large model at a fraction of the cost and latency. It satisfies every stated requirement (≥92% accuracy, ≤300 ms), so the extra point from the large model is not worth a 15× cost difference.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt caching: reduces the cost of the repeated prompt prefix only. Every request still pays large-model output and latency.
• Provisioned Throughput: buys capacity, not a cheaper model, and at this steady volume the large model stays far more expensive.
• Overnight batch: the discount is real, but live moderation needs a result within 300 ms, which batch cannot provide.

Key takeaway: choose the smallest model that meets the quality bar. Distillation and fine-tuning exist to move narrow tasks onto cheaper, faster models.

Q001446.stem: Twenty product teams call three model providers: Amazon Bedrock and two external LLM APIs. Security wants provider API keys held centrally rather than by teams. Finance wants per-team quotas and chargeback, and the platform team wants automatic fallback to another provider during outages. Which design meets all of these requirements?

choices.text: Create a Bedrock application inference profile per team and use it for all three providers
Let each team store the provider keys in its own Secrets Manager secret and tag the secrets for cost allocation
A central GenAI gateway holding keys, enforcing quotas, and routing with fallback
Apply SCPs that restrict which Bedrock models each team account may invoke

Q001446.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A gateway is the one place every call passes through. It can hold the provider credentials (teams never see them), enforce per-team quotas (for example, usage plans or custom counters), implement routing and fallback logic across providers, and emit per-team token and cost metrics for chargeback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-team secrets with tags: teams still hold the keys, and nothing enforces quotas or fallback. Tags on secrets don't measure token spend.
• Application inference profiles: a useful Bedrock cost-tracking tool, but they only cover Bedrock models, not the external providers, and they do no routing.
• SCPs on Bedrock models: a governance guardrail for Bedrock only. They provide no quotas, no chargeback, and nothing for external APIs.

Key takeaway: cross-provider key custody, quotas, routing, and chargeback are gateway concerns. Service-native features cover only their own service.

Q001451.stem: A GenAI summarization microservice on AWS Lambda must be exposed to 40 external partners. Each partner needs its own API key and daily request quota, malformed JSON bodies must be rejected before invoking Lambda, and AWS WAF must protect the endpoint. Which front door meets all requirements with the least custom code?

choices.text: An API Gateway REST API with per-partner usage plans, request validation, and a WAF web ACL
A Lambda function URL with IAM authentication, with request validation implemented in the function
An API Gateway HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, per-partner usage plans, and AWS WAF
An Application Load Balancer with the function as a target and WAF rate-based rules per partner IP

Q001451.explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway REST APIs natively support API keys with usage plans (throttling and quotas per key), request validators that check the body against a JSON schema model before the integration runs, and direct association with an AWS WAF web ACL, so no custom code is needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• HTTP API: cheaper and simpler, but HTTP APIs do not support API keys or usage plans, and they do not offer request validation like REST APIs, so the quota requirement fails.
• Lambda function URL: no API keys or quotas, and validation would be custom code inside the function.
• ALB with WAF rate rules: rate rules throttle by IP, not per partner key, and there are no quotas or API keys.

Key takeaway: per-client API keys, quotas, and request validation → API Gateway REST API. Simple JWT-protected routes at low cost → HTTP API.

Q001457.stem: Employees sign in to a corporate IdP through SAML. They use an internal GenAI web app whose browser code must call Amazon S3 and a Bedrock-backed API directly with short-term AWS credentials, each scoped so a user can reach only their own S3 prefix. No IAM users may be created. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: IAM Identity Center with a permission set assigned to each employee for the application's AWS account
An IAM user per employee, created automatically by SCIM provisioning from the IdP
Cognito user pool (SAML) plus identity pool with per-user scoped roles
A shared IAM user whose access key is embedded in the web app and rotated every 30 days

Q001457.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cognito user pools can federate with a SAML IdP, so employees keep single sign-on. The identity pool then exchanges the user pool tokens for temporary AWS credentials. The role's policy can use the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} variable to limit each user to their own prefix, all without IAM users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM Identity Center: gives workforce users access to AWS accounts and the console or CLI through roles. It is not designed to vend per-user, app-scoped credentials to browser code.
• IAM users via SCIM: violates the no-IAM-users rule and creates long-term credentials.
• Shared embedded key: exposes a long-lived credential to every browser, with no per-user scoping.

Key takeaway: app end users who need scoped temporary AWS credentials → Cognito (user pool + identity pool). Workforce access to AWS accounts → IAM Identity Center.

Q001465.stem: A data scientist in SageMaker Studio wants to compare four Bedrock models interactively. The Studio domain runs in VPC-only mode with no internet egress, which security will not change. Calls with boto3 hang and time out. What should the team do?

choices.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime and call the models from the notebook with boto3
Switch the Studio domain to public internet mode for the duration of the experiment
Add a gateway VPC endpoint for Bedrock to the Studio subnets' route tables
Build an API Gateway and Lambda layer for the notebook to call, since notebooks cannot reach Bedrock directly

Q001465.explanation:
Why this is correct:
In VPC-only mode, traffic to AWS APIs needs a private path. An interface endpoint (PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime provides one, and with private DNS enabled the SDK resolves the normal endpoint name to it. The notebook can then call the runtime API directly, which is the lowest-overhead option for exploration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• API Gateway and Lambda: unnecessary infrastructure for ad hoc work, and the notebook still would need a private path to reach that API.
• Public internet mode: security explicitly will not allow egress changes.
• Gateway endpoint: gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, not for Bedrock.

Key takeaway: SDK calls from a private VPC to AWS services need interface endpoints (or NAT). Gateway endpoints are only for S3 and DynamoDB.

Q001468.stem: Two hundred concurrent Lambda workers call a model API. When they receive a throttling error, each waits exactly 1 second and retries. Monitoring shows retries arriving in synchronized waves that keep triggering throttling. Which change best resolves this?

choices.text: Exponential backoff with jitter, capped delays, and limited attempts
Retry immediately and increase the maximum number of attempts so requests eventually succeed
Raise the fixed retry delay from 1 second to 5 seconds for all workers
Add a circuit breaker that permanently stops calls after the first throttling error

Q001468.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exponential backoff spreads retries over growing intervals, and jitter randomizes each worker's delay so retries stop arriving at the same moment. The cap and attempt limit keep latency bounded and avoid endless retry loops.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer fixed delay: all workers still wait the same amount, so the waves just arrive every 5 seconds instead.
• Immediate retries with more attempts: increases load on an already throttled service and makes the problem worse.
• Permanent circuit breaker: circuit breakers are useful, but opening permanently on the first throttle turns a transient condition into an outage. They should reset after a cooldown.

Key takeaway: fixed-interval retries synchronize clients. Add jitter to break the synchronization and backoff to reduce pressure.

Q001470.stem: A Bedrock agent must call an internal order REST API with 12 operations. The agent often picks the wrong operation or omits required parameters. The team also wants to generate client SDKs from the same API definition. What should the team provide?

choices.text: An IAM policy listing the allowed API actions, attached to the agent's service role
A natural-language description of all 12 operations in the agent's instructions, with parameter hints
A CloudFormation template of the API resources, uploaded as the action group definition
An OpenAPI schema for the action group with operation descriptions and typed, required parameters

Q001470.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock Agents action groups accept an OpenAPI schema. The agent uses operation descriptions to choose the right call, and parameter types and required flags to build valid requests. The same OpenAPI document can generate client SDKs and documentation, so one machine-readable contract serves both needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Natural-language instructions: loosely structured, and they don't enforce types or required fields. They also can't generate SDKs.
• IAM policy: controls authorization to AWS APIs, not the shape of calls to your own API.
• CloudFormation template: describes infrastructure, not request and response contracts. It is not a valid action group definition.

Key takeaway: a machine-readable API contract (OpenAPI) is how agents learn what they can call and with which arguments.

Q001471.stem: A three-person startup needs a React chat frontend for its Bedrock-backed API. Requirements: deploy on every Git push, a preview URL for each pull request, user sign-up and sign-in, and minimal infrastructure to manage. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: An EC2 instance running Nginx with a cron job that pulls the repository every few minutes
An S3 static website behind CloudFront with a CodePipeline per branch and a custom sign-in page
AWS Elastic Beanstalk running a Node.js environment with a separate environment per pull request
AWS Amplify Hosting connected to Git with pull request previews and Cognito-backed authentication

Q001471.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amplify Hosting builds and deploys web apps directly from Git, supports per-branch environments and pull request previews, and integrates with Cognito-based authentication. It covers every requirement with very little infrastructure for a small team to operate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 + CloudFront + CodePipeline: works, but PR previews, per-branch pipelines, and sign-in must be assembled by hand, which is much more to build and maintain.
• EC2 with Nginx: servers to patch and scale, no PR previews, and polling-based deployment.
• Elastic Beanstalk per PR: heavyweight environments for a static frontend, and slow and costly per preview.

Key takeaway: frontend hosting with Git-based CI/CD, previews, and built-in auth → Amplify.

Q001474.stem: A development team wants an assistant inside their IDE that can upgrade a Java 8 application to Java 17, generate unit tests for existing classes, and answer questions about AWS APIs, with administrators able to manage access centrally. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Q Developer in the IDE, with subscriptions managed centrally by administrators
Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer, which comments on pull requests with code quality recommendations
The Amazon Bedrock console playground, with prompts pasted from the IDE
Amazon CodeGuru Profiler, which identifies expensive lines of code in running applications

Q001474.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Q Developer integrates with popular IDEs. It provides code transformation (including Java version upgrades), unit test generation, code explanations, and AWS guidance, with subscriptions and access managed centrally by administrators.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeGuru Reviewer: reviews code in pull requests. It does not transform code or generate tests in the IDE.
• CodeGuru Profiler: analyzes runtime performance of deployed applications, which is unrelated to the requested tasks.
• Bedrock playground: a generic model sandbox with no IDE integration, no project-wide transformation, and no admin-managed developer subscriptions.

Key takeaway: developer-productivity AI in the IDE (transform, test, explain) → Amazon Q Developer.

Q001480.stem: An API calls a model to approve refunds, then writes the decision to a CRM. Clients time out after 30 seconds and retry, but sometimes the backend had already finished, so the CRM gets duplicate refund records. Which change prevents duplicates while keeping client retries?

choices.text: Set the model's temperature to 0 so a retried request produces the same decision
Disable client retries so each request is sent only once
Increase the client timeout to 120 seconds so fewer requests are retried
Client idempotency keys checked with a conditional write

Q001480.explanation:
Why this is correct:
An idempotency key identifies a logical operation across retries. On the first request, the backend records the key (for example, with a DynamoDB conditional write) together with the result. A retry with the same key returns the saved result instead of writing to the CRM again. This makes retries safe.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout: reduces how often duplicates happen but does not eliminate them, since network failures can still cause retries.
• No retries: removes resilience; transient failures would become user-facing errors.
• Temperature 0: a consistent decision is still written twice. The duplicate comes from the side effect, not from the model.

Key takeaway: any retried operation with side effects needs idempotency, regardless of how deterministic the model is.

Q001483.stem: A customer-facing Bedrock chatbot must block hate, violence, sexual, and insult content in both user inputs and model outputs. Product wants stricter blocking on inputs than on outputs, and the team must not write custom classifiers. Which configuration meets these requirements?

choices.text: A guardrail with contextual grounding checks at a high threshold for both prompts and responses
A guardrail with content filters for those categories, using separate strengths for prompts and responses
An Amazon Comprehend toxicity check in a Lambda function before and after each model call
A guardrail with a denied topic named 'hate speech and violence' and sample phrases

Q001483.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Guardrail content filters target exactly these harm categories and let you set filter strength separately for inputs (prompts) and outputs (responses). They are applied by passing the guardrail on each call, with no custom classification code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Contextual grounding: detects responses not supported by source content or not relevant to the query. It is a hallucination control, not a harmful-content filter.
• Denied topic: meant for business subject areas to avoid (for example, investment advice). It is a poor, incomplete substitute for purpose-built content filters.
• Comprehend in Lambda: possible, but it is custom integration code, which the team wants to avoid.

Key takeaway: harmful content categories → content filters; off-limits business subjects → denied topics; ungrounded answers → contextual grounding.

Q001500.stem: A company has two privacy needs. Need 1: redact customer names and phone numbers from each chat message in real time before it is sent to a model. Need 2: find out which of its 3,000 S3 buckets contain PII and keep that inventory current. Which assignment of services is correct?

choices.text: Comprehend (or guardrails) for need 1; Macie for need 2
Amazon Macie for both needs, since it detects PII in text and in S3
Amazon Comprehend for both needs, running batch PII jobs over every bucket for need 2
Amazon Macie for need 1 and Amazon Comprehend for need 2

Q001500.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Comprehend's PII detection works on individual text in near real time, which fits redacting each message inline. Guardrail sensitive information filters are another option in a Bedrock flow. Macie discovers sensitive data at rest across S3, with automated discovery and an inventory across many buckets, which fits need 2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Macie for both: Macie analyzes S3 objects and is not an inline API for redacting messages in a request path.
• Comprehend for both: you could build batch jobs, but you'd reinvent bucket inventory, sampling, and continuous discovery that Macie provides.
• Swapped assignment: each service would be used for the job it is not designed for.

Key takeaway: inline text redaction → Comprehend or guardrails; estate-wide S3 sensitive data discovery → Macie.

Q001506.stem: Auditors require, for each fine-tuned model version: intended use, risk rating, training data description, and evaluation results, tied to the exact version approved for production and exportable for review. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Rely on CloudTrail logs of the training and deployment API calls as the audit record
Document the details in AWS Glue Data Catalog table properties for the training dataset
Store the information as tags on the Model Registry model package version
Create a SageMaker Model Card per version, linked to the Model Registry version, and export it

Q001506.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Model Cards are structured documentation for a model: intended uses, risk rating, training details, and evaluation results. They can be versioned, linked to a model package in the Model Registry, and exported (for example, as PDF), which matches the audit requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Registry tags: short key-value metadata, not structured governance documentation with evaluation results.
• Glue Data Catalog properties: describe datasets, not a model's intended use or risk.
• CloudTrail: records who called which API and when. That's useful evidence, but not documentation of intended use or risk.

Key takeaway: governance documentation → Model Cards; version and approval tracking → Model Registry. Use them together.

Q001521.stem: Before any model is trained, a team must check whether one age group is under-represented in a lending dataset and whether approval labels are distributed differently between age groups. Which analysis fits this stage?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify post-training bias metrics computed on model predictions
SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift monitoring on the production endpoint
SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics such as class imbalance (CI) and DPL
SageMaker Data Wrangler quick model feature importance

Q001521.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pre-training bias metrics run on the dataset alone. Class imbalance measures under-representation of a facet (here, an age group), and DPL compares how often positive labels occur across facets. No trained model is needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Post-training metrics: require a trained model's predictions, which don't exist yet.
• Model Monitor bias drift: monitors a deployed endpoint over time, which is later in the lifecycle.
• Quick model feature importance: shows which features drive a simple model, not whether groups are imbalanced or labeled differently.

Key takeaway: data-only fairness checks → pre-training metrics; prediction fairness → post-training metrics; production → bias drift monitoring.

Q001538.stem: A retailer generates 2 million product descriptions with an LLM. Only about 1% change per day, when products are updated. The descriptions are shown to a global audience, and the goal is low latency worldwide and no model cost per page view. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput so each page view gets a fast model response
Store outputs and serve via CloudFront; change keys on update
Put a semantic cache in ElastiCache in one Region that matches similar product requests
Enable Bedrock prompt caching so repeated page views reuse the cached prompt prefix

Q001538.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The descriptions are effectively static content. Generate each one once, store it, and serve it from edge locations with CloudFront. Page views then cost no model calls and get edge latency. Versioned keys (or targeted invalidations) handle the 1% that change each day.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt caching: still invokes the model on every view. It only discounts the repeated prefix.
• Single-Region semantic cache: adds remote latency for global users and approximate matching for content that is exactly known.
• Provisioned Throughput: pays for capacity to regenerate content that doesn't need regenerating.

Key takeaway: if model output is reusable as-is, treat it as content. Cache the result, not the prompt.

Q001539.stem: A support assistant returns answers of about 800 tokens that take about 12 seconds to complete, and users abandon the page before seeing anything. The team may not change the model, answer length, or capacity. Which metric should the fix improve, and how?

choices.text: Time to first token, by streaming responses (ConverseStream)
Throughput: buy Provisioned Throughput so the model generates tokens faster
Total generation time: reduce maxTokens so every answer finishes sooner
Tokens per second: raise the temperature so the model samples faster

Q001539.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The problem is perceived latency. Users see nothing until the full answer completes. Streaming delivers the first tokens within about a second, and the rest continues to render, so time to first token and perceived responsiveness improve without changing the model, length, or capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower maxTokens: truncates answers, which changes answer length and was not allowed.
• Provisioned Throughput: a capacity change, which is not allowed, and it doesn't necessarily reduce time to first token.
• Higher temperature: affects randomness, not generation speed.

Key takeaway: for long generations, stream. Users judge speed by time to first token, not total time.

Q001545.stem: A code-generation assistant must give stable, near-identical output for the same prompt, and a marketing-copy generator should vary its phrasing on each run. Which configuration is MOST appropriate, and what caveat applies?

choices.text: Set top_k to 0 for both so sampling is disabled and every run is fully reproducible
The same default temperature for both, because sampling parameters barely affect variation
High temperature for both, and fix the random seed so code outputs repeat exactly
Low temperature/top_p for code, higher for copy; temp 0 isn't a guarantee

Q001545.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Temperature and top_p control how much the model explores less likely tokens. Low values make output more focused and repeatable, which suits code. Higher values increase variety, which suits creative copy. Even at temperature 0, providers do not guarantee bit-identical output, so downstream checks should validate structure or behavior, not exact strings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• High temperature with a seed: high temperature works against stable code output, and seed support and determinism vary by model.
• Same default for both: sampling parameters are the main lever for variation.
• top_k = 0: its meaning differs by model (it may not disable sampling at all), and it would also remove the variety marketing wants.

Key takeaway: tune sampling per use case, and design tests for 'stable enough' rather than exact determinism.

Q001550.stem: A Bedrock-based application's error rate has doubled. The team must quickly tell whether the cause is capacity limits or malformed requests from a recent client release. Which CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace distinguish these causes directly?

choices.text: InvocationThrottles for capacity limits versus InvocationClientErrors for malformed requests
Invocations for capacity limits versus OutputTokenCount for malformed requests
InvocationServerErrors for both, split by model ID
InvocationLatency for capacity limits versus InputTokenCount for malformed requests

Q001550.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock publishes throttled requests separately (InvocationThrottles) from client-side errors such as validation failures (InvocationClientErrors). A rise in throttles points to quota or capacity. A rise in client errors right after a release points to the new client sending bad requests.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency and input tokens: latency can rise for many reasons, and token counts don't indicate whether requests are malformed.
• Invocations and output tokens: volume and output size don't separate the two causes.
• Server errors: represent service-side failures, a third category, not capacity limits or client mistakes.

Key takeaway: split errors by type (throttles, client errors, server errors) before debugging. Each points to a different owner and fix.

Q001554.stem: A healthcare GenAI app must let auditors review, for 7 years, every request where a guardrail intervened, including the input, the output, and which policy acted. Records must not be alterable. Which approach meets these requirements?

choices.text: Model invocation logging to a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket protected by S3 Object Lock
Rely on CloudTrail management events, which record each InvokeModel call and its guardrail result
Use the guardrail's CloudWatch metrics, which count interventions per policy type
Log interventions in the browser client and upload the logs nightly

Q001554.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model invocation logging captures request and response data (including guardrail trace information) to S3 or CloudWatch Logs. Delivering to an encrypted bucket with Object Lock retention meets the 7-year, tamper-resistant requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail management events: record API activity metadata, not the prompt or response payloads auditors need to review.
• Guardrail metrics: counts show how often interventions happen, not what was blocked for each request.
• Client-side logs: incomplete, controllable by users, and not trustworthy audit evidence.

Key takeaway: payload-level auditing → invocation logging; API activity auditing → CloudTrail; trends → metrics. Retention and immutability come from the log destination.

Q001559.stem: A release gate scores candidate chatbot models on relevance, factual accuracy, and consistency across paraphrased prompts. Model B has the higher average score, but its factual accuracy on a policy-question subset fell below the accepted level. Which evaluation design would have caught this correctly?

choices.text: Replace automated scoring with a weekly human spot check of 20 random conversations
Per-dimension (and per-slice) thresholds; composite only for ranking
Use a single weighted average of the three dimensions as the release gate
Measure factual accuracy only, since a factually correct answer is also relevant and consistent

Q001559.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Averages hide failures: a strong score on one dimension can mask an unacceptable drop on another, or on a critical slice such as policy questions. Per-dimension thresholds (and per-slice thresholds for high-risk topics) turn each requirement into its own gate. A composite is still useful for choosing among models that pass.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single weighted average: exactly how model B passed despite failing accuracy on policy questions.
• Accuracy only: a correct answer can still ignore the question or vary across paraphrases.
• Small weekly spot check: too small and too late to gate releases reliably.

Key takeaway: gate on each must-have dimension and critical slice; rank on the composite.

Q001573.stem: An agent's final answers are correct 95% of the time, but traces show it often calls the payment tool twice and uses nine tool calls where three would do. Which evaluation approach would detect these problems?

choices.text: Trajectory evaluation comparing the tool-call sequence and arguments against expected paths
End-to-end latency percentiles per session
Counting how many guardrail interventions occur per session
Final-answer correctness scoring against a golden dataset

Q001573.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trajectory evaluation looks at how the agent reached the answer: which tools it called, in what order, and with which arguments. Duplicate payment calls and unnecessary steps are visible only at this level, even when the final answer is right.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Final-answer correctness: the answers are mostly correct, so this metric would look healthy while unsafe duplicate payments continue.
• Latency percentiles: might rise with extra calls, but they can't tell you which calls were redundant or unsafe.
• Guardrail counts: measure content-policy interventions, not tool-use behavior.

Key takeaway: for agents, evaluate the path as well as the destination, especially when tools have side effects.
